title: The Tortoise and the Hare
text: A Hare was making fun of the Tortoise one day for being so slow. "Do you ever get anywhere?" he asked with a mocking laugh. "Yes," replied the Tortoise, "and I get there sooner than you think. I'll run you a race and prove it." The Hare was much amused at the idea of running a race with the Tortoise, but for the fun of the thing he agreed. So the Fox, who had consented to act as judge, marked the distance and started the runners off. The Hare was soon far out of sight, and to make the Tortoise feel very deeply how ridiculous it was for him to try a race with a Hare, he lay down beside the course to take a nap until the Tortoise should catch up. The Tortoise meanwhile kept going slowly but steadily, and, after a time, passed the place where the Hare was sleeping. But the Hare slept on very peacefully; and when at last he did wake up, the Tortoise was near the goal. The Hare now ran his swiftest, but he could not overtake the Tortoise in time.

title: The Lighthouse Keeper
text: Every evening, just before the sun dipped below the horizon, Mara climbed the one hundred and twelve steps to the lamp room at the top of the lighthouse. The climb never got easier, but she had done it for so many years that her legs knew the rhythm without her having to think about it. At the top, she checked the great lens, wiped away the salt that had gathered on the glass during the day, and waited for full darkness before lighting the lamp. The light itself was not large, but the lens bent and focused it into a single powerful beam that swept slowly across the water, visible for miles in every direction. Ships passing far out at sea depended on that beam to know where the rocks lay hidden beneath the surface. Mara rarely saw the sailors she helped, and they never saw her, but she liked to imagine them on deck, watching the light appear and disappear as the beam turned, and feeling a little less alone in the dark. When storms came, the wind howled around the tower and rain lashed the windows, but the light kept turning all the same. That was the whole of her job, she thought: to keep something small and steady burning, no matter what the night brought with it.

title: The River Road
text: The road to the coast followed the river for nearly forty miles, curling along its banks through fields, forests, and the occasional cluster of houses that called itself a town. Elin had walked it once before, as a child, holding her father's hand and complaining about her feet long before they had covered even a third of the distance. This time she walked it alone, with a pack on her back and no particular hurry to arrive anywhere by a certain hour. The first few miles were easy, flat ground beside slow-moving water, and she passed the time watching herons stand motionless in the shallows, waiting for fish that never seemed to come. By midday the river had narrowed and quickened, and the road climbed away from the bank into hills covered in old pine forest. The air smelled different here, sharper, and the sound of the water below was replaced by wind moving through the trees. She stopped for lunch on a flat rock overlooking a bend in the river where the current folded back on itself in slow circles. An old man fishing nearby nodded to her but said nothing, and she was glad of the silence. There was a kind of conversation that happened without words between people who had chosen, for their own reasons, to be alone in the same quiet place, and she had come to prefer it to most conversations that used words at all. In the afternoon the road dropped back down toward the water as the valley widened, and small farms appeared on either side, their fields marked off by low stone walls that had clearly been standing for a very long time. Smoke rose from a few chimneys even though it was not yet evening, and the smell of woodsmoke drifted across the road on the breeze. By the time the light began to turn gold and long shadows stretched out from the trees, Elin could see the first rooftops of the coastal town in the distance, and beyond them, a thin grey line that she knew was the sea. She did not hurry the last few miles. She had left home to walk this road at her own pace, not to arrive as quickly as possible, and there would be time enough, once she reached the water, to decide what came next.
